title: The early church, looking back
tomorrow: a window made of broken pieces. why does it glow?

cards: Saying what you actually believe can cost a little: a comment, an unfollow, a weird look at lunch. In Acts it costs Stephen everything. Stones are flying, and he says two things out loud.
“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And then, kneeling: “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” Nearby, the crowd's coats lie at the feet of a young man named Saul.
So, one question for today: what's worth saying out loud?

teach.b: The early church answers with one word from Acts. Jesus tells his friends, “ye shall be witnesses unto me.” Looking back, they witnessed three ways.

teach.h: A LIFE LAID DOWN, A LIFE GIVEN AWAY.
teach.b: With a life laid down: Stephen, and others tradition remembers, like Perpetua, a young mother in North Africa, and Polycarp, a bishop who would not curse Christ.
With a life given away: tradition says a young Egyptian named Antony heard a Gospel line read in church, “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor,” did it, and went into the desert to pray.
And with a voice joined to other voices: the creeds, short statements of faith meant to be said together. Now a neighbor who says it out loud too.
When a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first, Jesus answers with Israel's own words, the Shema, from Deuteronomy.
In the Jewish Publication Society's translation: “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
Deuteronomy says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up, and Jewish prayer keeps them evening and morning.
Shared ground: a short line about who God is, said aloud, sometimes at great cost. And one honest difference.
The Christian creeds go on to confess God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Jews hear the Shema's oneness without a Trinity. Two peoples, each saying it in their own words.

how: Churches that keep a calendar of saints remember Stephen, Perpetua, Polycarp and Antony on their feast days, and some congregations say the Nicene Creed together at Sunday worship; Jews say the Shema in evening and morning prayer.

games.q: your little sister asks why people at church say the creed together, instead of each saying what they personally believe. what does the early church suggest?
o: it's only an old habit, with no real reason behind it.
a creed is witness said with other voices, carrying each other.
it's so nobody can tell who doesn't believe it.
games.why: the creeds were made to be said together, out loud: one of three ways the early church witnessed, beside lives laid down and lives given away.

practice: Stand up, the way some congregations stand to say what they believe together.
Say one early name quietly, Stephen, Perpetua, Polycarp or Antony, or a saint your own church remembers, and stay standing for a few breaths with the one thing they did that you'd want to carry.
Then sit for the bell; if you pray, give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: The early church. Martyrs, monks and creeds: people who told what they had seen, with their lives and with their voices.

orig.note: Greek: witnesses, people who tell what they have seen. Acts 1:8: ye shall be witnesses unto me.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the first witnesses, and the young man holding the coats becomes one of them. Until tomorrow.
